summary: Screwpile light at the Wicomico River entrance on the Potomac, 1889 to 1940; the keepers' house burned in 1939 and an automatic light stands on its foundation.

structures.note: Square wooden keepers' house on five iron screw piles. The house was severely damaged by fire in 1939 and dismantled in 1940; the foundation carries a small automatic light (archive; LighthouseFriends).

access.note: The archive lists the station as not open to the public.

visit.note: The keepers' house is gone; no source describes a visit.

events.note: Congress appropriated $15,000 for a lighthouse at Cob Point Bar on 2 October 1888 (Board report, as LighthouseFriends quotes it)
Square wooden dwelling on five iron screwpiles erected 5-30 November 1889 (LighthouseFriends)
Fixed white fourth-order light first shown on the night of 25 December 1889
Red sector added on 15 August 1893 to mark lumps in the Kettle Bottom Shoals, with the Lower Cedar Point light
Additional red sector established on 10 April 1894 to cut a buoy and a Dukehart Channel buoy (LighthouseFriends)
Keeper O. O. Johnsen and assistant Robert Kuhn assisted two men with a disabled lumber-laden power boat, 13 April, and gave them shelter
Keeper Ole O. Johnson and assistant George H. Cullison assisted five people in a disabled motor boat, 22 September (LighthouseFriends)
800 tons of riprap deposited on the southeast side as an ice breaker against ice carried by the Potomac's ebb tide
Repairs made to the metal substructure (fiscal 1921)
Bulletin index for 1924-1929 lists the station as used in aerial navigation (Bulletin p. 135; the year is not given; the index covers 1924-1929)
Keeper O. O. Johnsen and assistant W. A. Gibbs rescued five persons adrift in a small skiff on 26 June during a heavy gale
Assistant keeper Thomas J. Steinhise helped the boat Demo, aground near the station with passengers, in October (LighthouseFriends)
Fire on 7 December 1939 severely damaged the superstructure; a Coast Guard board found the origin unknown (LighthouseFriends)
Automatic light established on the screwpile foundation after the fire (LighthouseFriends)
Keepers' house dismantled; the foundation serves a small automatic light

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The record gives 'deactivated 1940' and 'inactive', while the OpenStreetMap point is standing. The archive says the keepers' house was dismantled in 1940 and its foundation serves a small automatic light. LighthouseFriends says an automated light was established on the screwpile foundation after the 1939 fire, and that a modern light is shown there today. The 1940 'first lit' is that light on the old foundation, not a new station.

The archive's position (38 deg 14.27 min N, 76 deg 49.41 min W) is about 0.6 km from the OpenStreetMap and LighthouseFriends points, which match the present foundation. The archive gives positions only to the minute.
The Board's reports write 'Cob Point Bar'; the archive and LighthouseFriends write 'Cobb Point Bar'. The story uses 'Cobb' and notes the Board's spelling.

notes_for_editor: Fire of 1939: the Coast Guard board and the claim for Jennette's property are known only through LighthouseFriends, which quotes a bill and the board's finding; neither was read directly. Chronicling America searches for 'Cobb Point Bar' in Maryland and DC papers, 1939-40, returned nothing. 1927 rescue: the Bulletin's OCR reads 'O. Johnson' and garbles the station name ('PanBar'). I matched the passage to Cobb Point Bar by the keeper and assistant names, the June 26 date and LighthouseFriends' account of the same event. Check the page image (PDF p. 35) before publishing the keeper's name. 1914: the Bulletin prints 'O. O. Johnsen', as the archive does; LighthouseFriends prints 'Johnson'. 1928 Demo rescue: LighthouseFriends only. The Bulletin index for 1924-1929 lists Thomas J. Steinhise as having assisted a vessel (p. 269), without the details. The 1885, 1887, 1888 and 1889 Board reports are quoted through LighthouseFriends; the local corpus holds Board reports only from 1891, so those quotations are not checked against the originals. The 1893 red sector: arranged in the report for fiscal 1893 (scan p. 121) and shown from 15 August 1893 (fiscal 1894 report, scan p. 312). The 'used in aerial navigation' item is the Bulletin index's own entry; the passage it points to (p. 135) was not read. The archive spells the first assistant 'Alaska D. Jennett' and LighthouseFriends 'Jennette'; the story uses the archive's spelling. The Commissioner's fiscal 1920 and 1921 reports are read from the Internet Archive volume (scan pp. 544 and 655); the scan pages were confirmed against the report headings. The archive position is about 0.6 km from the present foundation and is not proposed as a correction. Verification pass 2026-10-28: the 1927 Bulletin prints the keeper as 'O. Johnson' (archive: Ole O. Johnsen); the story says so. The 1893 Bulletin's OCR for the red-sector sentence is damaged ('An-angements', 'seiitor'); the story quotes nothing from that sentence, and the phrase 'in conjunction with one in the Lower Cedar Point light' is used. The 1885 Board recommendation says $15,000 and the 1887 repetition says $25,000 (both as LighthouseFriends quotes them); the story states the difference. Roster: roster.py output matches the research JSON exactly (42 lines, including person slugs). The 1914 and 1927 Bulletin pages were checked by PDF page (19 and 35); the 1921 and 1920 Commissioner passages by scan page (655 and 544). The 1893 red sector arrangement is from the fiscal 1893 report, scan p. 121, and the 15 August 1893 change from the fiscal 1894 report, scan p. 312.
